title: Beyond Leaderboard Ranks: Selecting Software Engineering Agents Under Budget Constraints
trick: Re-price every leaderboard run from its token log, paired-test neighbours on shared tasks: most accuracy-cost frontier steps are statistically unresolved, and successive halving finds a cheap tie for 6.6% of full evaluation spend.
framing_stripped: Called 'budget-constrained agent selection' with an 'uncertainty-aware selection target' and 'decision-oriented agent evaluation'; it is a re-analysis of the public HAL trace archives (58,197 run-task records, 379 of 380 archives, 11 benchmarks, 7 retained) in three parts: (RQ1) an exact McNemar test with Benjamini-Hochberg correction on every pair of runs sharing the same tasks, which finds 27 of 35 steps along the seven accuracy-cost Pareto frontiers unresolved and, on SWE-bench Verified Mini (34 runs, 48 shared tasks), a $34.16 run 14.6 points behind the $170.78 leader that the tasks cannot separate (sec. IV, Fig. 1); (RQ2) a recomputation of every run's dollar cost from its token counts at one price sheet, which puts published HAL costs at up to 11.7x the reconstructed figure (cache tokens apparently counted twice; 16 o3 runs at an old $10/$40 sheet give 5.0x) and shows that evaluating only mid-difficulty tasks under-estimates full-benchmark cost by 20.4% on SWE-bench (sec. V, Table III); (RQ3) a replay of five evaluation-purchasing policies on the fixed historical matrix, where successive halving reaches the selection target $Q = 0.80$ for $353.62 of a $5,399.89 exhaustive SWE-bench spend (6.55%) with advance knowledge of each cell's cost, and leads on only four of seven benchmarks without it (sec. VI, Table IV). 'Rather than introducing a new optimization algorithm, our contribution is an empirical assessment of the evidence and evaluation strategies needed for budget-constrained agent selection.' (sec. I).
method_equations: Data (sec. III-A; Table I). Each HAL run (an executed configuration: model, scaffold, parameter settings; repeated executions of the same configuration stay as separate rows) is a row and each task a column; cell $(i,j)$ holds the binary outcome $Y_{ij} \in \{0,1\}$ and reconstructed cost $C_{ij}$. Four of 11 benchmarks are dropped for incomplete outcome or token records; for the rest, only tasks shared across runs are kept, runs with outcomes on fewer than half their traced tasks or non-positive cost are removed, and a missing or non-positive cell cost is imputed as that run's median positive cell cost. Result: 20,633 cells across 262 runs; SWE-bench Verified Mini keeps 34 runs on 48 of its 50 tasks (per-run accuracy moves at most 2.33 pp, no strict pairwise ranking reversed). Table I ($k$ runs, $n$ tasks, % unresolved pairs after BH, unresolved/all frontier steps, floor $100 \cdot 6/n$ pp): SWE-bench Mini 34, 48, 40.1, 3/4, 12.5; USACO 15, 307, 21.9, 0/4, 2.0; SciCode 38, 65, 100.0, 2/2, 9.2; CORE-Bench 61, 45, 67.5, 7/8, 13.3; GAIA 35, 165, 32.4, 7/9, 3.6; TAU Airline 47, 50, 79.8, 6/6, 12.0; AssistantBench 32, 33, 100.0, 2/2, 18.2. Cost reconstruction (sec. III-B, Eq. 1): per model call, with $I$ the inclusive input tokens, $R$ cache-read tokens, $W$ cache-write tokens, $O$ output tokens and $p_I, p_R, p_W, p_O$ their per-token prices, $$C = (I - R - W)\,p_I + R\,p_R + W\,p_W + O\,p_O;$$ provider token fields are normalised first; 'When cache usage is available only at the run level, we allocate cached tokens across tasks proportionally to their prompt-token counts.'; each model is priced at its latest fitted period (rates recovered by regression for 14 model identifiers, assumptions elsewhere); API token spend only. Paired test (sec. III-C): exact two-sided McNemar test on $Y_{ij}$ versus $Y_{i'j}$ over shared tasks, BH correction at $q = 0.05$ within each benchmark, 5,371 pairwise comparisons; 'unresolved' = not rejected (not equivalence). A frontier step joins adjacent Pareto runs ordered by cost. Resolution floor (sec. IV-B): if two runs disagree on $m$ tasks all in one direction, $p = 2 (1/2)^m$, so $m \ge 6$ is needed at $\alpha = 0.05$ and the smallest resolvable observed gap is $6/n$ (12.5 pp at $n = 48$); simulated 80%-power minimum detectable gap with observed disagreement patterns, 20.7 pp on SWE-bench (Table II: Exact / Boot. / Bonf. unresolved %, Within $\pm 10$ pp %, MDE pp = 36.9 / 33.2 / 62.6 / 4.8 / 20.7 for SWE-bench Mini; TAU Airline 68.1 / 64.0 / 96.4 / 0.2 / 30.2; AssistantBench 100.0 / 94.6 / 100.0 / 47.8 / 22.8). Budgets (sec. III-D): $E = \sum_{i,j} C_{ij}$ is exhaustive evaluation cost ($5,399.89 on SWE-bench); evaluation budgets 1, 2.5, 5, 10, 25% of $E$; deployment cap $d$ at the 25th, 50th, 100th percentile of true complete-run costs; a policy recommends the run with highest estimated accuracy whose estimated complete-run cost ($n$ times observed mean cell cost; unobserved runs get prior accuracy 0.5 and pooled mean cost) is at most $d$. Selection score (sec. III-E, Eq. 2): with $b_d$ the most accurate truly affordable run and $\mathcal{U}_d$ the truly affordable runs whose BH-corrected difference from $b_d$ is unresolved ($b_d$ included), $$Q = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\rm valid}|} \sum_{d \in \mathcal{D}_{\rm valid}} \mathbf{1}[\hat{i}_d \in \mathcal{U}_d],$$ where $\hat{i}_d$ is the selected run and $\mathcal{D}_{\rm valid}$ the caps with a recommendation; also an all-caps score (no recommendation = failure), true affordability, regret vs $b_d$, exact-best. 300 replicates per condition; 200 replicates over ten budgets (0.5-40% of $E$) interpolated for the first crossing of $Q = 0.80$. Policies (sec. III-F): random cell, random task, round robin, cheapest first; successive halving (SH) with equal dollar targets per surviving run, eliminating the lower-scoring half each round, unobserved runs ranked last; mid-range filtering (MR) spending 10% on random probes then buying tasks with estimated pass rate 0.30-0.70 (an oracle variant uses true rates); row-level EZR (best-vs-rest Naive Bayes over model id, family, provider, reasoning effort, scaffold, token prices; starts from up to four complete runs, then one run at a time); cell-level Distance-to-Heaven (D2H, Eq. 3): $$d_i = \sqrt{\frac{(1 - \tilde{a}_i)^2 + \tilde{c}_i^2}{2}}, \qquad s_i = \frac{w_i}{\sqrt{n_i + 1}},$$ with $\tilde{a}_i$ the min-max normalised observed accuracy of run $i$, $\tilde{c}_i$ the min-max normalised $\log(1 + \hat{c}_i)$ of its estimated complete-run cost $\hat{c}_i$, $n_i$ its purchased cells, $w_i = 1$ for the $\max(1, \lfloor \sqrt{k} \rfloor)$ runs of smallest $d_i$ among $k$ candidates and $0.15$ otherwise; runs visited in descending $s_i$, an unseen task drawn uniformly. Cost visibility: primary replay with advance cost checks (exact $C_{ij}$ seen before purchase), a prospective replay without (costs seen after purchase, overruns allowed). Results. RQ2 (sec. V-A): over 333 runs the published-to-reconstructed cost ratio has median 1.00, 95th percentile 5.00, maximum 11.7; two Anthropic runs at 11.7x and 9.9x ('logged token totals are consistent with cached tokens being counted twice'), one reported at $1,789.67 vs $180.13 reconstructed; 42 extracted runs lack recoverable token records. Sampling bias (sec. V-B, Table III, median estimated/true complete-run cost at 10% budget, 100 replicates; SWE / USACO / SciCode / CORE): oracle MR 0.796 / 0.986 / 0.822 / 0.834; probed MR 0.973 / 0.994 / 0.991 / 0.934; random tasks 0.985 / 0.992 / 0.909 / 0.933; oracle MR with separate uniform cost probe 1.006 / 1.007 / 0.848 / 1.037; on SWE-bench the 20 tasks with pass rate below 0.30 cost $4.38 per cell vs $2.59 for the 27 mid-range tasks (1.69x). RQ3 (Table IV, interpolated spend in USD to $Q = 0.80$ with advance cost checks; SH / Random / MR / D2H / EZR): SWE-bench Mini 353.62 / 755.98 / 655.06 / 379.19 / 942.20; USACO 72.69 / 72.93 / 83.12 / 173.55 / not reached; SciCode 25.29 for all but EZR 36.73; CORE-Bench 744.44 / 1,292.27 / 1,528.52 / 931.82 / not reached; GAIA 1,171.54 / not reached / 4,174.73 / 1,214.07 / 2,371.57; TAU Airline 156.11 / 235.16 / 218.63 / 160.55 / 280.07; AssistantBench 81.87 / 200.61 / 158.50 / 140.32 / 124.48. Table V (SH at 25% budget; affordable %, regret pp, exact-best %): SWE-bench Mini 100.0, 1.4, 60.5; CORE-Bench 93.8, 3.2, 58.3; TAU Airline 99.8, 2.5, 58.0; GAIA 91.2, 0.8, 79.3. Without advance cost checks SH has the lowest actual spend on four of seven benchmarks; at a 10% SWE-bench budget every SH replicate overruns, mean $3.04 (sec. VI-C). Expected-improvement acquisition lowers SWE-bench $Q$ at 25% by 0.132 (95% CI $[-0.169, -0.097]$); cost-normalised D2H weights lower $Q$ to 0.925 vs 0.968 (sec. VI-D). Early stopping at threshold $\lambda (6/n)$ with $\lambda = 0.25$ saves 16.1 pp of budget and drops $Q$ from 0.756 to 0.614 (sec. VI-E).
load_bearing_assumption: That one historical run per configuration, scored on 48 shared tasks with a binary 'resolved' label, is the evidence a team would buy, and that a paired test across those tasks is the right unit of uncertainty. Three parts can fail. (i) Run-to-run noise is unmeasured: 'Only four repeated-configuration groups are available, limiting conclusions about agent execution variability' (sec. VII); if the same configuration re-run moves by several tasks out of 48, the McNemar test on one run per side understates the uncertainty, the frontier itself is a sample, and successive halving's elimination by observed accuracy after a few cells is eliminating on noise. The paper's own example that 'An execution of the same configuration approximately five hours earlier has substantially different reported costs despite similar reconstructed spend' (sec. V-A) is the only replicate it discusses, and only its cost. (ii) The cost is a reconstruction: 'Reconstructed costs rely on standardized pricing, cache-allocation assumptions, and occasional imputation.' (sec. VII); run-level cache tokens are spread over tasks in proportion to prompt tokens, missing cells take the run median, 42 runs have no token record, and 'Our reconstructed costs represent API token spend only; they exclude hosting, external tools, and human-review costs.' (sec. III-B). The 11.7x headline is the gap between HAL's published number and this reconstruction; which of the two is the invoice is not established in the text. (iii) The replay stands in for live evaluation: 'Budget policies operate on fixed historical outcomes rather than fresh agent executions.' (sec. VII) and the primary replay sees each cell's cost before buying it, 'an idealized setting because an agent’s actual token usage is generally unknown before execution.' (sec. III-F). The 6.6% figure holds under (iii); the prospective replay already moves SH from six-of-seven to four-of-seven.
weakest_component: The selection score $Q$ together with the advance-cost-check replay. $Q$ gives full credit for any affordable run whose difference from the best affordable run is unresolved, and by RQ1 almost everything is unresolved on the small benchmarks (SciCode and AssistantBench 100% of pairs, TAU Airline 79.8%, CORE-Bench 67.5%, Table I), so the target $Q = 0.80$ is reached 'at the first tested budget level' on SciCode by several policies and the paper itself says 'Their apparent tie therefore reflects the tested budget grid and limited statistical resolution' (sec. VI-A) and that $Q$ 'credits unresolved accuracy differences and omits caps without a recommendation, potentially favoring policies on low-resolution benchmarks' (sec. VII). The exact-best rate is the honest number and it is 60.5% on SWE-bench at a 25% budget (Table V). Second, the headline 6.55% is from the replay in which the policy inspects the exact historical cost of a cell before purchase; without it SH leads on four of seven and overruns on every SWE-bench replicate (sec. VI-C). Third, the Table IV spends are 'crossings of interpolated mean curves rather than statistically established differences in minimum evaluation cost' (sec. VI-A) and the compared policies 'reflect complete policy implementations rather than isolated algorithmic components' (sec. VII), with SH using soft per-run targets that can eliminate a run 'before their accuracy is measured, potentially disadvantaging expensive configurations' (sec. VII). Fourth, the single-run-per-configuration data: run-to-run variance, which decides whether a 48-task paired test is even the right instrument, is not in the data (four repeated groups). Fifth, 'HAL provides a convenience sample of agent executions' (sec. VII); the retained SWE-bench matrix is 34 runs, and the models and scaffolds in it are not enumerated in the text.
regime: Data: public HAL trace archives (huggingface.co/datasets/agent-evals/hal_traces), 379 of 380 archives, 58,197 run-task records over 11 benchmarks; 7 benchmarks retained as complete matrices, 20,633 cells, 262 runs (Table I). Primary: SWE-bench Verified Mini, 34 runs x 48 shared tasks (HAL's 50-task subset of the 500-task Verified set), exhaustive evaluation cost $5,399.89, mean cell cost $4.38 on the 20 tasks with pass rate below 0.30 and $2.59 on the 27 mid-range tasks; observed accuracy range shaded in Fig. 1, leader $170.78 per complete run, cheapest unresolved contender $34.16. Others: USACO 15 x 307, SciCode 38 x 65, CORE-Bench 61 x 45, GAIA 35 x 165, TAU-bench Airline 47 x 50, AssistantBench 32 x 33, with binary outcomes replacing native grading on AssistantBench (exact match), CORE-Bench and SciCode (task-level success). Models and scaffolds: not enumerated in the text; mentioned are two Anthropic runs (cache double count), 16 runs of OpenAI o3 (old $10/$40 per-million price sheet vs $2/$8 standardised), and 14 model identifiers with regression-recovered rates; four repeated-configuration groups in total. Outcome label: SWE-bench test-based 'resolved'. Statistics: exact McNemar, BH $q = 0.05$ within benchmark, 5,371 pairs; bootstrap and Bonferroni as checks; 90% bootstrap intervals within $\pm 10$ pp for 4.8% of SWE-bench pairs. Replay: 300 replicates per condition (200 for the $Q$ curves, 100 for Table III), budgets 1-25% of $E$ (0.5-40% for curves), three deployment caps, two cost-visibility settings. Compute: none beyond replay on stored matrices; no fresh agent runs. Venue: not stated; arXiv v1 16 Nov 2026, cs.SE, CC BY 4.0. Replication artifact: referred to repeatedly ('documented in our artifact', sec. III-B), URL unknown (not in text).
information_asymmetry: The leaderboard shows one point per run, (published cost, accuracy); the trace archive behind it holds the per-task outcome vector $Y_{ij}$ and the per-call token quadruple $(I, R, W, O)$. The paper is an existence proof of how much the point hides: from the outcome vectors it recovers paired disagreements, hence that 40.1% of SWE-bench pairs and 3 of 4 frontier steps are unresolved and that the floor of any 48-task comparison is 12.5 pp (20.7 pp at 80% power); from the token logs it recovers that two published costs are 11.7x and 9.9x their token value through cache tokens 'counted twice' and that 16 o3 runs carry a 5.0x price-sheet drift, and that the 20 hardest SWE-bench tasks cost 1.69x the mid-range ones per attempt, so an accuracy-sharpening sampler hides 20.4% of deployment cost. What the archive still does not hold, and a replicate would: (a) run-to-run variance of accuracy and cost for one configuration, 'Only four repeated-configuration groups are available' (sec. VII); the one replicate discussed shows the reported cost moving between two executions five hours apart while the reconstructed spend is similar (sec. V-A), and nothing is said about whether the 48 outcomes moved; without that number no one can say whether a 14.6-pp gap on one run each is a property of the agents or of the draw, nor whether successive halving at tight budgets, which eliminates on a handful of observed cells, is eliminating signal or noise. (b) Per-task cache usage where providers log it only per run; the proportional allocation is an assumption the log cannot check. (c) The patch itself: the leaderboard and the paper use the test-based 'resolved' bit, while 'some test-passing patches are incorrect or only plausible' (sec. VII); the trace holds the patch. Forward versus hindsight: the primary replay buys cells knowing $C_{ij}$, a live evaluator does not ('token consumption is generally unknown until an agent completes its task', sec. VI-C); the prospective replay shows the price of not knowing (SH leads on 4 of 7 instead of 6 of 7, every replicate overruns). Inference, not in the text: the per-call token sequence in the trace is exactly what a mid-run cost predictor would be trained on, so the hindsight gap could be measured as 'how many turns in before a task's final cost is predictable within x%', and the replicate gap as a HAL-scale re-run of a few configurations several times (a pass^k and cost^k study on the 48 tasks), the two instruments this paper's design most needs and does not have. The paper's own prescriptions point the same way: 'Agent leaderboards should report accuracy uncertainty alongside execution costs' and costs 'reported separately, with task-level token usage, cache accounting, and model pricing preserved for reproducibility' (sec. VIII).
occupies: Published: on the HAL trace archives (58,197 run-task records, 7 complete benchmark matrices, 262 runs), that 27 of 35 accuracy-cost Pareto frontier steps and 21.9-100% of pairwise run comparisons are unresolved under exact McNemar with BH correction, with the $6/n$ resolution-floor argument and simulated 80%-power gaps per benchmark (Tables I-II); that published HAL costs differ from standardised token-based reconstruction by a median 1.00, 95th percentile 5.00 and maximum 11.7x, attributed to cache double counting and old price sheets, with the reconstruction formula (Eq. 1); that mid-range-difficulty task sampling under-estimates complete-run cost by 20.4% on SWE-bench and 16.6% on CORE-Bench while a separate uniform cost probe removes most of the bias (Table III); and that cost-adapted successive halving reaches $Q = 0.80$ for 6.55% of exhaustive SWE-bench evaluation spend under advance cost checks, lowest on six of seven benchmarks, with EZR, D2H, mid-range filtering and random sampling as the compared policies and the result narrowing without advance cost checks (Tables IV-V). The paper states its own scope: 'Our software maintenance conclusions rest on SWE-bench alone.' (sec. I), no new algorithm, no fresh executions, and selection on a team's own backlog with patch review as outcome named as future work (sec. VIII-C).

theme_fit.why: directly answers the lane sentence on cost accounting and benchmark validity: a measured gap between published leaderboard cost and token-reconstructed cost (up to 11.7x, median 1.00 over 333 runs, sec. V-A), the $6/n$ floor that makes a 48-task SWE-bench comparison blind below 12.5 pp, and a dollar-budgeted evaluation-purchase study on HAL, the lane's named route; what it leaves open (run-to-run variance on the same configuration, prospective cost prediction) is the lane's reliability question

supplies a ground-truth method for the true cost structure of agentic workloads: the token-level reconstruction (Eq. 1) with cache read/write terms, the finding that cache accounting alone can inflate a reported cost 11.7x, and that the hardest SWE-bench tasks cost 1.69x more per attempt; no serving or systems lever is touched

limitations_as_complaints: I compare agents with one run each on 48 issues and cannot tell how much of a 14.6-point gap, or of my successive-halving eliminations after a few cells, is the agent and how much is the draw, because the leaderboard almost never re-runs a configuration: 'Only four repeated-configuration groups are available, limiting conclusions about agent execution variability' (sec. VII, Statistical validity); the one replicate I do discuss moved its reported cost between two executions five hours apart, 'An execution of the same configuration approximately five hours earlier has substantially different reported costs despite similar reconstructed spend.' (sec. V-A), and I never say whether its outcomes moved.

My budget-saving headline assumes I know what each agent-task evaluation will cost before I pay for it, and that I am buying from a frozen table rather than running agents: 'The primary replay assumes advance knowledge of individual task costs, which is generally unavailable in live evaluations.' and 'Budget policies operate on fixed historical outcomes rather than fresh agent executions.' (sec. VII, Replay and selection validity); 'In practice, multi-turn tool-use trajectories have unknown costs before completion' (sec. VIII-C), and when I drop the assumption every replicate overruns and my method leads on four benchmarks instead of six (sec. VI-C).

The dollar figures I use to call leaderboard costs wrong by 11.7x are themselves rebuilt from token logs under assumptions I cannot check against an invoice: 'Reconstructed costs rely on standardized pricing, cache-allocation assumptions, and occasional imputation. Incomplete traces and multi-model scaffolds further limit exact attribution.' (sec. VII, Cost validity); 'Our reconstructed costs represent API token spend only; they exclude hosting, external tools, and human-review costs.' (sec. III-B), 'Forty-two extracted runs lack recoverable token records' (sec. V-A), and 'Consequently, reconstructed dollar amounts support comparative analysis rather than exact historical invoices or future deployment quotes.' (sec. VII).
